title: What should you ask first in a product design case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a product design case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first who the product is for and what success means, because a design answer is only as good as the user and goal it is built around. The trap, on a platform with two sides, is designing for one side and forgetting the other: a feature that delights buyers can drive sellers or drivers away.
body:
The first question to ask

Who is this for, and what would success look like for the business?

Product design questions, common in product and tech interviews, ask you to design something for a set of users. "Design a feature to help people split restaurant bills" could aim at more people using a payments app, more payments per user, or happier restaurants. Each goal leads to a different design. Agree one goal and one main user group before you suggest anything.

How to build your structure

  1. Clarify what is being designed and why.
  2. Agree the goal.
  3. Identify the users (on a platform, both sides).
  4. List their pain points.
  5. Suggest solutions.
  6. Prioritise one.
  7. Describe a simple first version (a minimum viable product, or MVP).
  8. Say how you would measure success.

The steps mirror the product launch framework, applied to a single feature.

A worked example: splitting a restaurant bill

Goal. More people using the payments app, measured by bills split each month.

Users. Three groups: the person who paid, the friends who owe, and the restaurant.

Pain points. The payer chases friends and works out who had what. Friends forget, or feel awkward. The restaurant wastes time splitting cards at the table.

Solutions. Scan the receipt and let each friend tap their items; automatic reminders; pay at the table by QR code.

Prioritise. Start with the payer, whose pain is greatest and who brings the friends. Receipt scanning with tap-your-items solves the hardest part, working out shares, and each split invites friends who may not use the app yet.

Size it. Suppose the app has 2M monthly users and 10% split one $80 bill a month. That is 200,000 splits and 200,000 × $80 = $16M of payments a month. These numbers are illustrative; the point is to give the interviewer a sense of scale.

MVP and metrics. Scan, tap, request, with one reminder. Success: bills split per month and the share of friends who join the app after being asked to pay. Guardrail: complaints about unwanted reminders.

"Before designing anything, I'd like to agree the goal and the users. I see three groups here, and I'd start with the person who paid, because their pain is the biggest."

The trap most people fall into

Looking at only one side of a two-sided platform. On marketplaces, ride-hailing and delivery apps, every change for customers affects suppliers too. Faster delivery promises can squeeze drivers; cheaper fares can cut their pay. See network effects and platforms for why both sides matter.

The second trap is jumping to a fashionable solution. "Add an AI assistant" is not a design. A strong answer connects user problem, product choice, change in behaviour and measurement.

Weak: "I'd add an AI chatbot that answers questions about the bill."
Strong: "The payer's main pain is working out who owes what, so the first version is receipt scanning with tap-your-items. I'd measure bills split per month and how many invited friends sign up."

Two prompts to try

A bank asks you to design a budgeting app.

Show the answer
  • User: pick a narrow group, such as graduates in their first job who struggle to predict bills before payday.
  • Job to be done: know how much they can safely spend without missing essentials.
  • First version: upcoming regular payments, a cautious safe-to-spend figure, alerts when planned spending exceeds the balance.
  • Measure: fewer missed payments among users, not just daily app opens.

The trap: designing for "everyone with a bank account".

Design a feature for a food-delivery app to reduce late orders.

Show the answer
  • Users: customers, restaurants and couriers.
  • Pain points: food not ready when the courier arrives; couriers waiting or sent far away; customers not knowing why.
  • Solutions: courier dispatch timed to the restaurant's real preparation time; live honest estimates for customers.
  • Measure: share of orders on time; guardrails on courier waiting time and restaurant cancellations.

Where to start: restaurants. If food is late, the fix lies in kitchen timing, not courier speed.

The trap: pushing couriers to ride faster.
